fixes.explanation: That's the plan, baker. The chief priests and scribes want Jesus arrested and killed, and they want it done on the quiet (Mark 14:1). Covert means hidden, like trying to swipe a cookie off the cooling rack while the whole family stands right there. It never works, but they're sure it will.

Not quite, friend. Mark 14:1 says they're looking for a covert way to arrest Jesus and kill Him. Then they say, “…or there may be a riot among the people.” (Mark 14:2) A crowd is what they're worried about, and that's like hiding a batch of cookies on a table in the middle of the room.

Yep, a riot. The chief priests and scribes say, “But not during the feast, or there may be a riot among the people.” (Mark 14:2) So their plan has a calendar problem. They're sneaky, but they still have to wait for the right time, like me waiting on the timer to ding before I open the oven.

That's exactly it. She broke open the jar and poured the perfume on Jesus' head (Mark 14:3). Once a jar is broken open, there's no closing it back up. It's like me tipping a whole jar of sprinkles over a batch, friend, because there's no scooping them back.
Nope, no gift for the house. Mark 14:3 says the woman broke open the jar and poured it on Jesus' head. Simon the Leper's home is the place where it happens. Jesus' head is where the perfume goes.

Close on the setting, since it all happens in Simon the Leper's home. But Mark 14:3 says she broke open the jar and poured it on Jesus' head. So the jar was opened, not left sitting there unopened. And the perfume went on His head.

Good guess pulling a number, but it isn't the one here. At this table, the grumblers say the perfume could have been sold for “…over three hundred denarii…” (Mark 14:5). A denarius is a coin, and they're figuring the price out fast.

Not the priests, friend. The grumblers say the perfume could have been sold “…and the money given to the poor.” (Mark 14:5) The chief priests show up in verses 1 and 10 of this passage, but the grumblers' words here are about the poor.

That's what Jesus says, baker. “She has done what she could to anoint My body in advance of My burial.” (Mark 14:8) She poured out the perfume, and Jesus told them what it meant. Burial is the word He uses.

Quiet is the opposite of what Jesus says. “…wherever the gospel is preached in all the world, what she has done will also be told in memory of her.” (Mark 14:9) The Twelve are the group Judas belongs to (Mark 14:10), and this promise reaches way past them. It goes to all the world, friend.

Nice picture, but Jesus doesn't say anything about a wall. He says, “…what she has done will also be told in memory of her.” (Mark 14:9) The promise reaches wherever the gospel is preached in all the world. That's a lot farther than one temple, baker.
Yep, money, friend. The chief priests “…promised to give him money.” (Mark 14:11) The text names money and stops there. It doesn't give a number in this passage, so I'm not going to make one up.
No land in this one, friend. The verse says they “…promised to give him money.” (Mark 14:11) Land isn't what the verse names. I think it's a sad one to read.
Not power, baker. Mark 14:11 says the chief priests “…promised to give him money.” Power isn't what the verse names. I think it's a heavy part of the story.
